tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

lastPrompt: What about a --squash to closing and if so remove "opening"?

message.content: Not true with --local

content.text:
You're right, I took it too broadly (I'm reading "not true" as my claim that every commit in a local cycle carries the same `ochid:`). That only holds for this cycle's form, `-s w` until the land with no agent commit in between. `--local` only means nothing is pushed, so `commit --local -s b` still makes an agent commit at each rung, and each work commit gets a different `ochid:`.

Squashing that ladder has the problem the rule describes, in both directions:
- **Work to agent:** the squashed commit keeps only one of the rungs' `ochid:` values, so the other agent commits lose their link from the work-repo.
- **Agent to work:** each agent commit's `ochid:` names its rung's change id, and most of those change ids disappear in the squash, leaving dangling references.

So being local isn't what makes a squash safe. It takes two separate conditions:
- **Nothing published:** no commit in the range is on a remote, so no published history is rewritten.
- **One agent link:** every commit carries the same `ochid:`, so no link is lost.

The refusal for different `ochid:` values already enforces the second condition, so the design holds. What changes is the rule's wording: the proposal should give those two conditions rather than exempt "a local cycle".

A `--local -s b` ladder would therefore be refused. Folding both sides together could make it work, by squashing the agent commits too and rewriting the trailers on both sides, but that's much more machinery, so I'd leave it out.

The plain version: `--squash` works only when nothing has been pushed and the whole ladder points at one agent commit, which `--local` alone doesn't guarantee.

content.text:
Agreed, `work` should be the default. Until the land, `-s w --local` is close to `-s por`: one repo, nothing pushed, and the agent side untouched. The one difference is that `-s w` stamps an `ochid:`, and that trailer lets the land connect the work to the agent's record.

`--scope` is required on `commit` today (`src/commit.rs:149`), so this is a real behaviour change. With local as the default too, a bare `vc-x1 commit --title ... --body ...` becomes a normal rung, and the worst outcome is an easily fixed local commit.

I'd make the default depend on what the commit is doing:

| Invocation | Default scope | Why |
|---|---|---|
| plain `commit`, `--opening`, `--closing` in a dual workspace | `work` | The agent side waits for the land. |
| the same in a plain repo | `por` | `work` doesn't exist there, and there's only one repo to choose. |
| `--push` | `both` | Pushing only the work side would publish an `ochid:` pointing at an agent commit nobody else can see. |
| `--land` | `both` | The land commits and stamps the agent side, and `vc-x1 land` already defaults to `both`. |

The rule behind the table is that building defaults to one repo and finishing defaults to both, and an explicit `-s` always overrides it.

`--push` is the one to get right, because a plain `work` default would make `commit --push` publish half a pair without saying so. `-s w --push` stays possible, but only if you ask for it, and it falls under the dangerous-combination guard already in the **commit works at every scope** Todo.

This also changes the flow's step 9, `vc-x1 commit -s b`, which the v0.3.1 proposal is already rewriting. The rule would then read as plain `vc-x1 commit` per rung and `vc-x1 land` at the end.

It isn't needed for rungs [4] to [8], so I'll file it as part of the **commit works at every scope** Todo in [4]'s commit unless you'd rather have it as a rung in this cycle.

The plain version: while a cycle is being built, a commit acts like one in a plain repo, with just a link back to the agent's record. Plain `vc-x1 commit` should do that by default, and only pushing or landing should involve both repos.

content.text:
**`[4]`:** that's the rung in this cycle's ladder, not the table: "[4] feat: commit and init stamp a URL-shaped ochid and ocid", the next piece of work. I should have spelled that out. It starts on your go, and "in [4]'s commit" just meant the Todo edit would be committed along with that rung.

**Scope:** I've taken your rules, so the table becomes:

| Invocation | `--scope` | Why |
|---|---|---|
| plain `commit`, `--opening`, `--closing` | optional, defaults to `work` | Local to one repo, and easily fixed. |
| `--push` | optional, defaults to `work` | Pushing doesn't change what any other bookmark contains. |
| `--land` | required | It merges into a different bookmark, so you have to say which repos. |

Three things follow from that:
- **Plain repos:** the `work` default becomes `por` there, as `work` doesn't exist in a plain repo.
- **`vc-x1 land` and `vc-x1 push`:** these should behave like `--land` and `--push`, since `land` and `push` are meant to work exactly like them. `land` currently defaults to `both` (`src/land.rs:88`), so that default goes and `-s` becomes required there too.
- **Guard:** I'm dropping my idea of treating `-s w --push` as a dangerous combination, because it's now the normal default.

One consequence to know about: after a default `--push`, the published work commit's `ochid:` can point at an agent commit that isn't on the remote yet. The link stays dead until the agent side is pushed, and pushing the agent side fixes it without rewriting anything, so it's a temporary gap rather than damage.

I'll record this in the **commit works at every scope** Todo as part of [4]'s commit.

The plain version: committing and pushing act on the work repo unless you say otherwise. Landing makes you name the scope every time, because it changes another bookmark.

3	//!
4	//! `commit`, `push`, and `squash` resolve the same two paths from
5	//! `-s` and `-R`, whatever side the scope names, since a half still
6	//! needs the other repo to find or name its partner, take the same
7	//! `jj op` snapshots before their mutation window and restore both
8	//! repos from them on a failure inside it, and read the pair's
9	//! state the same way: the work commit's trailer, and where its
10	//! partner stands. The description helpers they share are in
11	//! `desc_helpers`.

rand = "0.10"
rand_chacha = "0.10"
serde_json = "1"

[target.'cfg(unix)'.dependencies]
libc = "0.2"

Every writer now stamps `<url>#<chid>`, so hand-written trailers end here.

- `desc_helpers::ochid_value` is the one place a value is formed: the canonical URL, or the side's
  label for a repo with no hosted `origin`, which keeps local-remote workspaces and test fixtures as
  they were.
- `commit`, `push`, and `squash` read the URL from `origin`. `init` takes it from its plan, since the
  cross-link runs before `origin` is added, by `CrossRefSide`.
- `-s w` adds `ocid: <agent-url>/commit/xxxx` below the `ochid:`, none with no hosted URL. `-s b` and
  `init` stamp `ochid:` alone, my call. `push`'s partner commit names the work repo by URL, and
  stamps no `ocid:`.
- A rewrite keeps the `ocid:`: `--closing`'s finalize, `squash`'s re-describe, and `push`'s restamp,
  by `WorkCommit::ocid`. The text a partner shares and the opening's body leave it out.
- `fix-desc`'s inference of a missing trailer still writes the label, since published forms stay
  valid and it is a repair of old history.
- Not yet: an `ocid:` keeps `xxxx` until [feat: land sets the ocid trailer to the agent commit's
  SHA][6], so one published by `-s w --push` then `push` keeps it.
- Also records wink's scope decisions in **commit works at every scope**: `--scope` defaults to
  `work`, `--land` requires it, and `--closing --squash` as considered. None of that is built here.
- `--opening`'s help says the bookmark is pushed only with `--push`.

132:### Commit-body form
133-
134-The specimen is [commit-model.md](commit-model.md). A commit body is the [Problem-first
135-shape](#problem-first-shape) with one addition: a body whose
136-problem has several sub-problems arranges them by a fixed recursion, so a reader knows what any
137-bullet is from its marker and its depth. The earlier statement, "a problem statement then a solution
138-statement, both broad", left that arrangement to taste, and taste converged slowly and separately.
139-
140-- **An intro paragraph states the general problem**, and defines any word the title assumes. It is
141-  mandatory. [Prose form](#prose-form) wants it regardless, and a body opening on a bullet is a body
142-  a `--body` flag can mistake for an option. The problem is *this commit's*, never the cycle's: the
143-  cycle's problem lives in the In Progress block, and a body whose problems outnumber what the diff
144-  resolves is describing something larger than the commit.
145-- **`*` bullets are the problem's facets**: sub-problems that decompose the intro's general problem,
146-  not a grab-bag of unrelated fixes. A body reaching for unrelated problem bullets is usually asking
147-  to be more than one commit.
148-- **`-` bullets are solutions**, and every `-` sits under a `*`, solving that facet. A `-` with no
149-  `*` above it reads as a solution to nothing, so there are no top-level solutions: a solution that
150-  retires every facet at once is written under each, or the facets are one.
151-- **One facet is the trivial commit**: the intro, one `*`, one or more `-` under it. Not a second
152-  form, the general form at its smallest.
153-- **A bookend body is a pointer**: an opening or closing commit resolves no problem of its own, so
154-  its body is the intro paragraph alone, naming the cycle by its title and pointing at its record,
# Commit model

Two commit bodies from the `config loader` cycle in [cycle-model.md](cycle-model.md), shown as
specimens rather than a skeleton: a work rung's body and a bookend's. Copy the shape, not the
words. The rules are in [Commit-body form](prose.md#commit-body-form).

## A work rung

Title: `refactor: split loader from parser`

```
Config loading and parsing are one function, so the CLI cannot load a
config without parsing it and a test cannot parse one without a file on
disk. The move into its own module is what forces the split.

* The two jobs share one function and one error type.
  - `config::loader` finds and reads the file and returns the text with
    its path, so a caller that only wants to know which file was read
    stops there.
  - `config::parser` takes text and returns the schema, so a test hands
    it a string and never touches the filesystem.
* `main` still reaches into the parse result by field.
  - `main` calls `config::load` and receives the schema, so the field
    access moves behind the module boundary and the CLI no longer knows
    the file's shape.
```

The intro states this commit's problem and defines "split", the word the title assumes. Each `*`
is one facet of it, each `-` under a `*` answers that facet, and nothing names a file that the
diff already lists.
fix: commit stays local unless --push asks

A bare commit publishes what it makes, and --no-push leaves the
opening's bookmark to be pushed anyway, so keeping a cycle local takes
flags that are easy to forget, and forgetting one publishes it.

Solution: commit publishes nothing unless --push asks, the opening's
bookmark included, --local and its alias --no-push say so outright, and
the [commit] push key goes, so no workspace changes what a bare commit
does. See details in zDOING.md.

Rung [5] is ready for your review, and `vc-x1 validate` passes, including three new land tests.

**What changed**
- **Local by default:** `land` and `commit --land` now only move things on the machine. `--push` publishes as well, agent repo first, so `land --push` does what a land did before.
- **Agent commit:** the land commits the agent `@` with one `ochid:` per work commit that names it, oldest first. If none name it, as in a cycle of finished pairs, it makes no agent commit.
- **No fold after a land:** `push` publishes that agent commit as it is, and `squash` leaves it alone. Anything that arrives later stays in `@` for the next cycle.
- **`--closing --land -s b`:** the agent commit is now left to the land, so it names the rungs too.
- **Refusal:** landing below a commit that also names the agent `@` is refused before anything moves.

**Differences from what we discussed**
- **Remote bookmark:** you said land deletes the local bookmark and push deletes the remote one. I didn't build the push part, because `push` would then also delete a bookmark kept with `--skip remote`. A bare land leaves a published cycle's bookmark on `origin` and prints the `delete-bookmark` command, and `land --push` still deletes it. This doesn't affect this cycle, whose bookmark was never pushed. It's recorded as open in the Todo.
- **`land --push`:** you hadn't asked for this flag. I added it to match `commit --push`.

**Known gaps**
- `commit --land --dry-run` lists the agent commit's trailers without the closing, because the closing isn't made yet.
- A single-step cycle with `--no-url-trailer` still folds on push. That's harmless, as there's no `ocid:` to break.
- `ocid:` stays `xxxx` until rung [6].
- No test covers `--land --local` or a land from a commit `--closing` on a held-local ladder; the new tests use `vc-x1 land`.

]

Actually `vc-x1-dev` is the "development" not the -dev profile. Hmmmm that's confusing. A bare app name, `vc-x1` is the "released" version which could be built with any profile probably the "release" but could be anything. The "-dev" appending means development version which could be built with any profile. Actually, for "cargo build" there is never an issue with the name, the path is different. target/<profile>/<name>. For "dev" releasing we'll install as vc-x1-dev but for building the name is defined in cargo.toml. Soooo it seems `vc-x1 build --profile xyz` causes `cargo build --profile xyz` and `vc-x1 install --profile xyz` invokes `vc-x1 build ...`  and then it should do a `cargo install --path  <profile-path>` so it needs to figure out  the path. Not sure about what I wrote, is coherent but ask Qs and we'll figure out what to do.

Yes, that's coherent. Today one setting does two jobs: `[profile.dev]` holds both the cargo profile and `suffix = "-dev"`. You're describing two separate choices:

- **Build profile:** how it's compiled, which sets `target/<profile>/`. The binary's name there always comes from `Cargo.toml`.
- **Installed role:** `vc-x1` is the released version and `vc-x1-dev` the development version, and either can be built with any profile.

So the change I just made is wrong, because it maps the name `vc-x1-dev` to the `dev` profile. It's uncommitted and nothing has been installed; `vc-x1-dev` is still the [4] build.

**One correction:** `cargo install --path` won't fit, for three reasons:
- It takes the crate's directory, not a profile's output directory.
- It does its own build rather than installing the one you just built, so the binary you tested isn't the one installed.
- It can't install under another name, so it can't produce `vc-x1-dev`.

Questions, each with my recommendation:

1. **How do you choose the role?** I'd default to the running binary's role, so `vc-x1-dev install` installs `vc-x1-dev` and `vc-x1 install` installs `vc-x1`. An explicit flag would override that, perhaps `--as dev|release`. `install --dev` exists only as a retired flag that gets refused, so it could be brought back if you prefer it.
2. **What is the default profile for each role?** I'd use `dev` for development and `release` for released, with `--profile xyz` overriding either. Is that right, or should `[build] default-profile` apply to both?
3. **How is the binary installed?** I'd keep the current `cp` to a `.new` file followed by `mv`. It copies the binary you built and can name it anything, and it can safely replace a binary that's running, which is the case in `vc-x1-dev install`.
4. **Where does the path come from?** Cargo's rule is simple apart from one exception: `dev` builds into `target/debug`, and any other profile into `target/<profile>`. But `[build] commands` isn't cargo-specific, so I'd keep `bin` as a config key and move only `suffix` out of the profile, for example to `[install] dev-suffix`. Do you want `vc-x1` to work for non-cargo projects too? If not, `bin` can be worked out and dropped.
5. **Should a released install be stricter?** Today `install` reports a suffixed version, a commit not on `main`, or a dirty build. I think those should be errors for `vc-x1` unless forced, and only notes for `vc-x1-dev`. Those checks would then follow the role rather than the profile.
6. **Where does this work go?** I'd take it out of [5], reverting my install edits and filing the design as a Todo to run as its own cycle, with `vc-x1 install --profile dev` still working until then. It changes the config format and `[5]` doesn't depend on it. The habit of installing after each code-changing rung stays in the proposal either way.

(wink + agent, 2026-10-30) `[profile.dev]` holds both how a binary is built and what it is installed
as, so `vc-x1-dev` reads as the `dev` profile. Wink's model: they are two choices. The profile is how
it is compiled, `target/<profile>/<name>`, the name from `Cargo.toml`. The role is what it is: bare
`vc-x1` the released version and `vc-x1-dev` the development version, either from any profile.
`build` and `run` take a profile alone, and `install` alone has a role. Historically the install was
`cargo install --path . --locked`, sometimes with `--root` and a copy, before profiles existed.

A proposal, the agent's, nothing decided:

- `[role.released]`, `default-profile = "release"`, and `[role.development]`, `suffix = "-dev"` and
  `default-profile = "dev"`. `suffix` leaves `[profile.*]`, and `[install] commands` says
  `{role.suffix}`.
- `install --as released|development`, the default the running binary's role by its name, so
  `vc-x1-dev install` stays development, and `--profile` overrides the role's default.
- A released install refuses a dirty build, a commit not on `main`, and a suffixed version unless
  `--force`, where today it only reports them. A development install reports them.
- The copy stays configured: `[install] commands` holds `cp {profile.bin}` and `mv`, or a project may
  list `cargo install --path . --locked --profile {profile.cargo} --root <dir>` and copy from
  `<dir>/bin`, which needs no path rule and, by cargo's help, shares the workspace's target directory.
  `bin` stays either way, since `run` needs it and `[build] commands` is not cargo-specific.
- A config with `suffix` under a profile is refused naming the move, or read as the role's for a
  while. Open.

content.text:
The install edits are reverted, with no differences left in those files, and the design is filed in `TODO.md` as **install has a role and a profile**. `vc-x1 validate` passes, and `vc-x1-dev` is now the current [5] code (`0.85.18-5`, dirty).

**A correction to my last message:** I overstated the case against `cargo install`. Its help says that with `--path` it uses the workspace's target directory, and it accepts `--profile`, so it shouldn't be a separate build of the code. It still can't install under the name `vc-x1-dev` by itself, but your old `--root` and copy method solves that.

## Proposal

Install gets two independent choices, and `build` and `run` keep only the profile:

```toml
[role.released]
default-profile = "release"

[role.development]
suffix = "-dev"
default-profile = "dev"

[profile.release]
cargo = "release"
bin = "target/release/vc-x1"

[profile.dev]
cargo = "dev"
bin = "target/debug/vc-x1"

[install]
dir = "~/.cargo/bin"
commands = [
  "cp {profile.bin} {install.dir}/vc-x1{role.suffix}.new",
  "mv {install.dir}/vc-x1{role.suffix}.new {install.dir}/vc-x1{role.suffix}",
]
```

| Command | Role | Profile | Installs |
|---|---|---|---|
| `vc-x1 install` | released | `release` | `vc-x1` |
| `vc-x1-dev install` | development | `dev` | `vc-x1-dev` |
| `vc-x1-dev install --profile release` | development | `release` | `vc-x1-dev`, optimized |
| `vc-x1 install --as development` | development | `dev` | `vc-x1-dev` |

- **Default role:** it comes from the running binary's name, and `--as` overrides it. That is the only thing the name decides.
- **Released installs are strict:** `vc-x1` refuses a dirty build, a commit not on `main`, or a suffixed version unless you pass `--force`. A development install only reports them, as it does today.
- **Keep the string substitution:** `.vc-config.md` still holds the commands, so only `{profile.suffix}` becomes `{role.suffix}`.
- **`cp` or `cargo install`:** the default stays `cp {profile.bin}`, the binary `validate` and `build` just produced. A project can list `cargo install --path . --locked --profile {profile.cargo} --root <dir>` and copy from `<dir>/bin` instead, with no code change. `bin` stays either way because `run` needs it.

I'd run this as its own cycle after this one lands. The one open point is what happens to an existing config with `suffix` under a profile: refuse it and name the move, or accept it for a while. I lean towards refusing, since only this project's small family of repos would be affected.

After committing the agent `@`, a Land now replaces the `xxxx` in each work commit's `ocid:` with that
commit's SHA, so the links work once published.

- Each commit from the trunk to the target whose `ochid:` names the agent commit and whose `ocid:` is
  a placeholder is re-described, oldest first, by change id, and its tree is checked unchanged. A
  failure restores the work repo.
- The trunk moves to the target by change id, since the rewrite changes the target's SHA.
- It keys on the agent `@-`, not on the commit just made, so a Land stopped partway finishes on a
  rerun. A value already set is left.
- A published commit keeps its placeholder, with a warning, since this would rewrite it, my call. A
  rung published by `-s w --push` is the case, its agent commit already made by `push`.
- `push`'s own partner commit sets no SHA, so a `-s w --push` ladder keeps `xxxx`. Only a Land sets it.

Rung [6] is ready for your review. `vc-x1 validate` passed with the 3 new tests, and after a final one-line test-comment fix I reran the fast validation, which also passed. The new `vc-x1-dev` is installed. A dry run of the land on this cycle changed nothing and showed what you'd expect: an agent commit naming all six work commits, oldest first, then the `ocid:` set on each.

**What changed**
- **SHA stamping:** after committing the agent `@`, the land replaces `xxxx` with that commit's SHA on each work commit that names it. Change ids stay the same, and a test confirms the trees and `ochid:` trailers don't change.
- **Tree check:** the land also compares each commit's tree after the rewrite. If one changed, it restores the work repo and stops.
- **Trunk move:** the trunk now moves by change id, because the rewrite changes the tip's SHA.
- **Rerun:** a land that stopped partway should finish the remaining `ocid:` values when run again, and it leaves values already set alone. No test covers this rerun.

**Two behaviours you may want to overrule**
- **Published commits:** a published commit keeps `xxxx`, with a warning, because stamping it would rewrite it. That was my call, and you've said pushed work is still fluid, so you might prefer it rewritten.
- **`-s w --push` ladders:** these keep `xxxx` for good, because only a land sets the SHA and those commits are already published by then.

Also, with no closing yet, the dry run took the agent commit's text from the latest rung. In the real land it will come from the closing commit.

**The stand-in:** yes, `xxxx` is a stand-in, and yes, `vc-x1-dev commit -s w` adds both trailers without anything by hand, as it did for [4] and [5]. Two exceptions: `-s b` stamps `ochid:` only, and a repo with no hosted `origin` (or `--no-url-trailer`) gets the label `ochid:` and no `ocid:`.

One difference from what you wrote: the real value doesn't need an agent-repo push, only the agent commit. Its SHA exists once that commit is made, so the land stamps it locally. The link just returns a 404 until the agent repo is pushed, which is why the agent repo goes first and nothing may fold into that commit afterwards.

**Overwriting:** there's no single parameter that does this. Here's what exists today:

| To change | On | Command | Limits |
|---|---|---|---|
| Title and body | `@-` | `vc-x1 squash -s w --title ... --body ...` | Needs both flags, and also folds a non-empty `@` into `@-`. Keeps `ochid:` and `ocid:`. |
| Title only | any revision | `vc-x1 fix-desc -r REV --title ... --no-dry-run` | No body option. |
| `ochid:` | any revision | `vc-x1 fix-desc -r REV --no-dry-run` | Only repairs a bad value, and can't set one you choose. |
| `ocid:`, or any trailer you choose | any revision | none | Only a hand-run `jj describe`, which is what I used on the early rungs. |

`commit -r REV` looks like the natural one, but it refuses any commit that already has an `ochid:` trailer and points you to `squash`.

**My proposal:** add `--overwrite` to `commit -r`:

```
vc-x1 commit -r REV --overwrite [--title T] [--body B] [--ochid V] [--ocid V]
```

- Anything you leave out is kept, so you can change just the body or just one trailer.
- It only re-describes the commit, with no folding, and the tree is checked unchanged.
- A published commit is refused unless `--yes` is given.
- It ends the need to run `jj describe` by hand on trailers, and `squash --title --body` could then be retired.

It's not built. I'll file it as a Todo in [6]'s commit, to run after this cycle lands alongside the install work.

The two behaviours in my last message, published commits and `-s w --push` ladders keeping `xxxx`, are still yours to overrule.

content.text:
Yes, `desc` is a better home than my `commit -r --overwrite`. `desc` is already the command for a commit's description, `commit` keeps its one job of making commits, and with none of the new flags it reads exactly as it does today. I've filed it in `TODO.md` as **desc takes a title, body, and trailers**, to run after this cycle lands; it isn't built yet.

```
vc-x1 desc -r REV [--title T] [--body B] [--ochid V]... [--ocid V]
```

Any combination works, and anything you leave out is kept.

`desc` currently accepts a range, `-n`, and `-s both`, and defaults to `@`. That's fine for reading but risky for writing, so I'd add these rules, which are recorded in the Todo as still to be agreed:

- **One commit, one repo:** a write needs an explicit `-r` naming one commit, so the default `@` or a range can't be overwritten by accident. `-s both` is refused, because each repo's trailers are its own.
- **`--ochid` repeats:** a land's agent commit carries several, so the flag can be given more than once, and whatever you give replaces all the existing `ochid:` lines.
- **Removing a trailer:** `--ocid ""` removes the line.
- **Description only:** nothing folds, and the tree is checked unchanged.
- **Safety:** a published commit is refused unless `--yes`, and `--dry-run` prints the result without writing.
- **Retiring the old routes:** `squash --title --body` and `fix-desc --title` would go, and `commit -r`'s refusal would point to `desc` instead.

input.content:
A work commit's ocid holds a placeholder until the agent commit it links
exists, and nothing replaces it, so a landed cycle's links lead nowhere.

Solution: after committing the agent @, a Land sets each placeholder to
that commit's SHA, oldest first by change id, each tree checked
unchanged, and moves the trunk by change id since the rewrite changes
the tip's SHA. A published commit keeps its placeholder, with a warning.
See details in zDOING.md.

[package]
name = "vc-x1"
version = "0.85.18-6"
edition = "2024"

# The package name is the installed binary's name and never
# changes: a cycle's validation installs under its own root,
# `--root tmp/dev` in `.vc-config.md`'s `[validate]` lists, so a
# dev build (a suffixed version) never replaces the stable
# `vc-x1` on the PATH. The promotion is the plain `cargo install`
# from `main`. Before 2026-10-20 a cycle renamed the package to
# `vc-x1-dev` instead, guarded by build.rs (chores-16, 0.78.3).

[lints.clippy]
# The process-spawn ban: `Command::new` is disallowed via
# clippy.toml's `disallowed-methods`, and deny (not warn) so a bare
# new spawn site fails `cargo clippy` even without `-D warnings`.
# The documented allowlist lives in clippy.toml.
disallowed_methods = "deny"

[dependencies]
chrono = { version = "0.4", default-features = false, features = ["now"] }
clap = { version = "4.6", features = ["derive", "wrap_help"] }
clap_complete = { version = "4.6", features = ["unstable-dynamic"] }
futures = "0.3"
# The gix jj-lib 0.46 resolves (no features of our own): the
# session's lock-contention downcast needs type identity with the
# errors jj-lib returns, and init's bare-repo creation reuses it.
gix = { version = "0.88", default-features = false }
# When raising jj-lib: check whether it now offers the commits a
# remote's bookmarks are on without fetching. If so, `git_command`
# in src/jj/session.rs and its two callers take it, and
# clippy.toml's register entry 6 closes (TODO.md > ## Waiting).
jj-lib = "0.46"
log = { version = "0.4", features = ["std"] }
pollster = "1.0"
# The rng jj-lib's `SecureConfig` takes to mint a repo's config id,
# at jj-lib 0.46's versions so the types are its own, seeded the way
# jj-cli seeds it (src/jj/session.rs `load_repo_config`).
rand = "0.10"
rand_chacha = "0.10"
serde_json = "1"

[target.'cfg(unix)'.dependencies]
libc = "0.2"

## Cross-repo Linking with Git Trailers

Commits in each repo use [git trailers](https://git-scm.com/docs/git-interpret-trailers) to
cross-reference their counterpart in the other repo. The `ochid` (Other Change ID) trailer contains
a workspace-root-relative path and jj changeID:

```
ochid: /.claude/xvzvruqo   # points to a .claude repo change
ochid: /wtpmottv            # points to an work repo change
```

Paths always start with `/` (the workspace root, i.e. vc-x1). Each repo has a `.vc-config.md` that
identifies its location within the workspace, so tools can resolve these paths locally.

For full details see:
- [Git trailer convention](./notes/chores/chores-01.md#git-trailer-convention)
  - [ochid (Other Change ID)](./notes/chores/chores-01.md#ochid-other-change-id)
  - [ChangeID path syntax](./notes/chores/chores-01.md#changeid-path-syntax)

file.content:
`[repos] work` and `[repos] agent`. The agent one may be any reachable relative path, under
  the work-repo's tree or outside it, and the `.claude` in the label is a constant that says
  nothing about it, so a sweep over the agent-repo's directory leaves every trailer alone.
- Which label a commit takes is decided by reading a repo's own `.vc-config.md`, its
  `[repos] agent` resolved relative to that file and compared against the directory holding it.
  So the config picks the side and the label is a constant, and the two never need to agree.
- `ochid: /<chid>` references a change in the **work-repo**.
- `ochid: /.claude/<chid>` references a change in the **agent-repo**.

Trailers are blank-line-separated `key: value` lines at the end of the commit body, using the chid's
**12-character** prefix:

```
ochid: /.claude/xvzvruqowktp   # points to an agent-repo change
ochid: /wtpmottvxqzl           # points to a work-repo change
```

How many, and which direction:

- **Work-repo commits** each carry one `ochid: /.claude/<agent-chid>`, the agent-repo's change ID.
- **The agent-repo commit** carries one `ochid: /<work-chid>` per work-repo commit in that push. The
  count is per *push*, not per cycle. A trapezoid close-out whose rungs were pushed 1:1 as they
  landed still carries exactly one. More than one occurs when a single push publishes several
  work-repo commits.

Use `vc-x1 chid -s work,agent -L` to capture the change IDs (first line work-repo, second agent
repo).

`ochid:` trailers are **stamped by `vc-x1 push`**. Never hand-write them into a commit body or
`--title`/`--body`.

cross-reference their counterpart in the other repo. The `ochid` (Other Change ID) trailer contains
a workspace-root-relative path and jj changeID:

```
ochid: /.claude/xvzvruqo   # points to a .claude repo change
ochid: /wtpmottv            # points to an work repo change
```

Paths always start with `/` (the workspace root, i.e. vc-x1). Each repo has a `.vc-config.md` that

input.new_string:
cross-reference their counterpart in the other repo. The `ochid` (Other Change ID) trailer contains
the other repo's URL and a jj changeID:

```
ochid: https://github.com/winksaville/vc-x1.agent-session#qrxovvvqxnrq   # an agent repo change
ochid: https://github.com/winksaville/vc-x1#xwvlonzwkzpo                 # a work repo change
```

The URL comes from the repo's `origin`, normalized to https with any user, password, port, and
`.git` dropped, so ssh and https clones stamp the same value. It is the change ID and not a SHA, since
a SHA changes on every rewrite, so `vc-x1` resolves it, in the workspace's repo when the URL names
one, and GitHub knows nothing of it.

A work half made by `commit -s w` also carries `ocid` (Other Commit ID), a link a browser can follow:

```
ocid: https://github.com/winksaville/vc-x1.agent-session/commit/xxxx
```

`xxxx` stands in until a Land commits the agent repo and sets the SHA, and the link resolves once the
agent repo is pushed. `commit -s b` and `init` stamp `ochid` alone. It is a display convenience, and
`ochid` is what the tools resolve.

A repo with no hosted `origin`, a local path or none, and `--no-url-trailer`, stamp the side's label
and no `ocid`:

```
ochid: /.claude/xvzvruqo   # points to an agent repo change
ochid: /wtpmottv           # points to a work repo change
```

Published labels stay valid for good. `/` is the workspace root, `/.claude` always means the agent
repo whatever its directory is called, and `/.agent-session/`, the directory's own name, is accepted
beside it. `validate-desc` also reports a URL naming another repo, and `fix-desc` reports it without
rewriting it, since a renamed repo would otherwise have all its history rewritten.

ochid: https://github.com/winksaville/vc-x1#xwvlonzwkzpo                 # a work repo change
```

`.git` dropped, so ssh and https clones stamp the same value. It is the change ID and not a SHA, since
a SHA changes on every rewrite, so `vc-x1` resolves it, in the workspace's repo when the URL names
one, and GitHub knows nothing of it.

A work half made by `commit -s w` also carries `ocid` (Other Commit ID), a link a browser can follow:

```
ocid: https://github.com/winksaville/vc-x1.agent-session/commit/xxxx
```

`xxxx` stands in until a Land commits the agent repo and sets the SHA, and the link resolves once the
agent repo is pushed. `commit -s b` and `init` stamp `ochid` alone. It is a display convenience, and
`ochid` is what the tools resolve.

A repo with no hosted `origin`, a local path or none, and `--no-url-trailer`, stamp the side's label
and no `ocid`:

```
ochid: /.claude/xvzvruqo   # points to an agent repo change
ochid: /wtpmottv           # points to a work repo change
```

Published labels stay valid for good. `/` is the workspace root, `/.claude` always means the agent
repo whatever its directory is called, and `/.agent-session/`, the directory's own name, is accepted
beside it. `validate-desc` also reports a URL naming another repo, and `fix-desc` reports it without
rewriting it, since a renamed repo would otherwise have all its history rewritten.

file.content:
## Suffix scheme

The cycle (opening -> commits -> closing, per the [Cycle protocol](../AGENTS.md#cycle-protocol))
encodes each commit's phase in the version suffix, the **final identifier `0` marking a
Preparation**.

This is the manifest's own spelling, read by whoever inspects `Cargo.toml` or `-V` output. It is not
a name for a step: a step is identified by its title, and an in-flight ladder rung carries neither a
number nor a version (see [Steps are named, not numbered](prose.md#steps-are-named-not-numbered)).
The identifiers below count commits within a phase, and nothing dereferences one.

- `X.Y.Z-0`: Preparation
- `X.Y.Z-1`, `X.Y.Z-2`, ...: the commits between
- `X.Y.Z`: Close-out (bare version, no suffix)

**Preparation is optional.** A lightweight cycle, with no ladder and no setup commit, skips `-0` and
starts at `-1` (its first commit). A single-step cycle is one commit, the Close-out, and carries the
bare `X.Y.Z` ([Cycle shape](../AGENTS.md#cycle-shape)). The same holds at every level: a sub-cycle
needing no Preparation omits its `.0` (see Nesting). One that grows a Preparation later adds the `0`
step without renumbering siblings.

input.new_string:
Readers first, then writers, then the Land. Every reader takes `<url>#<chid>`, and a URL is checked
against the repo's `origin`, canonically. `commit`, `init`, `push`, and `squash` stamp it, and a work
half alone adds `ocid: <url>/commit/xxxx`, while `--no-url-trailer` and a repo with no hosted `origin`
keep the label. A bare `commit` and a bare Land stay on the machine and `--push` publishes. A Land
commits the agent `@` with one `ochid:` per work commit naming it, sets each placeholder `ocid:` to
its SHA, and folds nothing into it. The rules' change is drafted in **agent-files(proposal): v0.3.1**
rather than made here.

against the repo's `origin`, canonically. `commit`, `init`, `push`, and `squash` stamp it, and a work

commits the agent `@` with one `ochid:` per work commit naming it, sets each placeholder `ocid:` to
its SHA, and folds nothing into it. The rules' change is drafted in **agent-files(proposal): v0.3.1**
rather than made here.

I think this is better than what I built, with one gap to decide. A work commit would carry:

```
ochid: qrxovvvqxnrq
ocid: https://github.com/winksaville/vc-x1.agent-session/commit/<sha>
wurl: https://github.com/winksaville/vc-x1
```

An agent commit would carry only `ochid: <work-chid>`, once per work commit. `wurl` is a placeholder name.

**Why it's better**
- **`ochid` gets simpler:** it always means "the other repo", so the side label and the URL never told a tool anything it needed. The repo-checking code moves to `ocid`, where the URL already is.
- **Nothing is lost on the work side:** `ocid` says where the agent repo lives, even while its SHA is still `xxxx`. If the SHA goes stale, its repo URL plus `ochid` still find the commit.
- **Renames do less harm:** a renamed repo only affects the convenience links, and `ochid` never goes stale.
- **The work repo stands alone:** if the agent repo is deleted, you lose the context but no work history.

**Things this changes or leaves open**
1. **The work URL can't include a SHA:** a commit can't contain its own hash, so it can only name the repo. Its value is showing where a commit originated once it's been forked or copied, and that's a good reason to have it.
2. **Every paired commit now needs `ocid`:** it's the only thing naming the agent repo, but `-s b` and `init` currently stamp `ochid` alone. They can commit the agent side first, since the work chid is already known, and stamp the real SHA straight away. That only holds if nothing folds into the agent commit afterwards, so `-s b` loses its fold on push.
3. **An agent clone alone can't find its work repo:** a bare chid doesn't say where to look. That fits the work repo being the root, but the agent commit then has no pointer back unless its config supplies one.
4. **The third-repo case is lost:** the Problem section mentions a transcript commit naming a `vc-x1-messages` commit, and a bare `ochid` can't do that. If that matters later, an agent commit could add a URL trailer only for that exception.
5. **Readers need one small change:** `validate_ochid` has to accept an empty prefix. `extract_bare_id` should already handle a bare chid, but I haven't checked. Published `/.claude/<id>` and `/<id>` trailers stay valid, and URL-form `ochid` values exist only on this unlanded cycle.

**Timing**
Do it before the land. Once landed, URL-form `ochid` values would be permanent history that readers must support forever. Right now they're only on the pushed topic bookmark, which you've said is still fluid.

It would add a rung ahead of the land: the stamping changes, reworking rungs [1], [2] and [4], and a rewrite of this cycle's trailers, in the same pass as the `set_ocids` fix. `--no-url-trailer` would then mean omitting `ocid` and `wurl`.

**Decisions for you**
- Should the third trailer be on every work commit, or only where the origin differs? I'd put it on every commit, because a forked commit can't add it after the fact.
- What should it be called? I'd avoid `wurl` if it might also name the agent's repo, and `orepo` or `origin-url` might read better.

The plain version: `ochid` becomes just an ID, the URLs become separate links only the work repo carries, and the land should wait until that's done.

I agree, with one change to the order: code before descriptions. Your five points first:

1. **Parents:** this is better than a bare repo URL, because it names both the repo and a real commit. I'd call it `pcid`, one line per parent, so a trapezoid gets two:
   ```
   ochid: qrxovvvqxnrq
   ocid: https://github.com/winksaville/vc-x1.agent-session/commit/<sha>
   pcid: https://github.com/winksaville/vc-x1/commit/<parent-sha>
   ```
   Inside the repo it repeats what git already records. It pays off when a commit is forked or cherry-picked, because the trailer still shows where it came from. The catch is that stamping a parent changes its SHA, so a land has to go oldest first, setting `ocid` and `pcid` in one pass.
2. **Agent first:** agreed. `-s b` then gets a real SHA immediately, while `-s w` keeps `xxxx` until the land. Either way, nothing may fold into an agent commit afterwards.
3. **`.vc-config` on both sides:** that closes the gap for an agent-only clone. I haven't checked whether the agent's config records the work repo's URL, so it may need a key.
4. **`custom.md` trailers:** that covers the third-repo case. It adds one requirement: rewrites must keep trailers they don't recognize. Today `with_trailers` adds its lines after a blank line, so a custom trailer would end up in the body, separated from the rest.
5. **Code is the easy part:** agreed, so I'll stop weighing cost.

**Why code goes first**
The installed `vc-x1-dev` would flag a bare `ochid` in `validate-desc`, and the next commit would still stamp the old form. Doing the code first means the new build can check the rewritten descriptions. I'd go in this order:

1. Remove the closing commit, since rungs shouldn't sit above it and it's fluid.
2. Add a rung with the new stamping, the readers, trailer preservation, and the `set_ocids` fix.
3. Add a rung that updates v0.3.1 and the README, because they describe the old form.
4. Re-close with the new build.
5. Rewrite the trailers on every commit in the cycle, keeping trees and change ids. This has to be by hand, as `desc` doesn't take trailers yet, so it's a recorded bend of **No hand-written trailers**.
6. Run `validate-desc` and `land --dry-run`, then force-push the bookmark on your go.

**Things to watch**
- **Commits won't match their own contents:** rewritten descriptions on rungs [1] to [4] will carry the new trailers, while those rungs' code and docs still implement the old ones. I think that's fine, because the trailer is metadata about the link and the record explains the change. I'd leave those rung titles alone, as they're true of what each rung did.
- **The cycle's title becomes wrong:** "feat: ochid trailers are URLs" would now say the opposite of the result. The bookends are being rewritten anyway, so I'd retitle them and the bookmark, perhaps to "feat: work commits link their partner and parents by URL". The opening's change id wouldn't change.
- **v0.3.1:** **ochid trailers are URLs** gets rewritten and renamed to match, including the rule that only work commits carry URLs and that agent commits carry `ochid` alone.

content.text:
Yes, it's doable, and I'd put it in a `vc-x1` subcommand. I'd only run it on `main` if we want a uniform history enough to break every old SHA reference.

**Does rebasing change `ochid`s?**
No. A rebase or re-describe changes the SHA and keeps the change id, and `ochid` holds a change id. `ocid` and `pcid` do change, because they hold SHAs. One thing to test on a clone: whether a fresh clone keeps the change ids of older commits, because I recall jj deriving them from the SHA when a commit has no stored change-id header.

**Can it update both repos?**
Yes, and the new protocol makes the order simple, because the references only depend one way:
1. **Agent repo first:** its commits name work commits by change id only, so nothing in the work repo needs to exist first. This fixes the agent SHAs.
2. **Work repo second, oldest first:** each commit gets `ocid` from the new agent SHA and `pcid` from its parents' new SHAs.

The trees don't change, and the program can verify that for every commit. It should run from outside any session, because a live agent is writing to the agent repo, and an earlier note says that repo is never rewound while running.

**What makes it harder than it looks**
- **Old SHA references go dead:** bodies, `notes/`, `zCLOSED.md` and the transcripts cite SHAs like `8be6ff7c`. Commit messages can be remapped, but changing files changes trees, and `notes/chores/` is frozen, so those citations would stay stale. GitHub links to old commits eventually 404 too.
- **Every clone and fork breaks:** `main` gets force-pushed in both repos, and anything pinned to a SHA in the family's other repos needs checking.
- **Commit dates matter:** `lookup` uses committer time to find partners when a commit has no trailer, so the rewrite must preserve those dates. Signatures, if there are any, would be lost.
- **Old data is messy:** of 661 commits, some are `lost`, `none`, or use 8-character ids, and `fix-desc`'s proposed repairs all point at one agent commit, which looks wrong. The program needs an explicit rule, and I'd leave those commits without an `ocid` rather than guess.
- **Performance:** rewriting commits one at a time rebases all their descendants each time, so it should be one jj-lib transaction. `git filter-repo` handles SHA maps well, but I'd expect it to lose jj's change ids.

**My opinion**
- **Build the tool:** with a dry run and a SHA map, it's also the answer to a problem this cycle left open, stale URLs after a repo rename.
- **Don't rewrite `main` for this change alone:** keeping the old forms readable takes very little code, while rewriting costs every historical SHA citation and breaks the v0.3.1 rule that published trailers are never rewritten. New commits can use the new protocol, with `/.claude/<id>` staying valid on old ones.
- **Try it on a clone first:** that shows what really breaks, and then the decision is yours with real numbers. If forks and outside links turn out not to matter here, a uniform history may well be worth it.

The plain version: the program is sound and both repos can be updated, since change ids survive. The real cost is breaking every old SHA reference, so I'd build it and trial it on a clone before deciding about `main`.

Yes, a new rung before the closing. Mechanically, I'd remove the closing and re-make it afterwards rather than slip the rung underneath it. The closing moved the record from `zDOING.md` to `zCLOSED.md`, so a rung's record edits beneath it would conflict with that move. The result is the same shape either way, and the agent repo isn't touched.

The ladder would become:

| Label | Rung | Version |
|---|---|---|
| [8] | new: the code for the modified trailer protocol | `0.85.18-8` |
| [9] | new: v0.3.1 and the README name the modified protocol | `0.85.18-9` |
| [10] | the closing, re-made and retitled | `0.85.18` |

The tool runs last, after the re-close, to update every commit including the closing, and then you'd have the force-push of the bookmark to approve.

**On `cycle --update`:** I'd go with a slightly different name, `vc-x1 trailers --update [-r RANGE]`, defaulting to the current cycle.
- **What it acts on:** it changes trailers, not the cycle, and `--update` alone doesn't say what it updates.
- **One engine:** the only difference between this cycle and the history tool I just filed is the range. So `-r main` later is the history rewrite, with no second command.
- **The land uses it too:** `set_ocids` and `pcid` stamping become the same oldest-first pass, which also fixes the published-commit problem from my notes.
- **No hand rewrite:** it replaces the hand-run trailer rewrite I'd planned, so that bend isn't needed.

The history tool is filed at the bottom of `## Todo`, uncommitted. The interruption landed before I updated the Continuation notes, so they still describe the old plan; I'll fix that when [8] opens.

52	/// A description with its `ochid:` trailer: the text, trailing
53	/// blank lines trimmed, a blank line, then `ochid: <value>`, so a
54	/// body read from a file ending in a newline gets one blank line
55	/// before the trailer, not two.
56	pub fn with_trailer(text: &str, value: &str) -> String {
57	    format!("{}\n\nochid: {value}", text.trim_end())
58	}
59	
60	/// A description with its `ochid:` trailer and, when there is one, the
61	/// `ocid:` trailer below it.
62	pub fn with_trailers(text: &str, ochid: &str, ocid: Option<&str>) -> String {
63	    let desc = with_trailer(text, ochid);
64	    match ocid {
65	        Some(ocid) => format!("{desc}\nocid: {ocid}"),
66	        None => desc,
67	    }
68	}
69	
70	/// A description with one `ochid:` trailer per value, in order, the
71	/// agent commit a Land makes for a whole cycle.
72	pub fn with_ochids(text: &str, values: &[String]) -> String {
73	    let trailers = values
74	        .iter()
75	        .map(|v| format!("ochid: {v}"))
76	        .collect::<Vec<_>>()
77	        .join("\n");
78	    format!("{}\n\n{trailers}", text.trim_end())
79	}
80	
81	/// What an `ocid:` trailer holds until the Land knows the agent
82	/// commit's SHA.
83	const OCID_PLACEHOLDER: &str = "xxxx";
84	
85	/// The `ochid:` value naming `chid`: by the repo's canonical URL when
86	/// `url` has one, else by the side's `label`, the form a repo with no
87	/// hosted `origin` stamps.
88	pub fn ochid_value(url: Option<&str>, label: &str, chid: &str) -> String {
89	    match url.and_then(crate::url::canonical_repo_url) {
90	        Some(url) => format!("{url}#{chid}"),
91	        None => format!("{label}{chid}"),
92	    }
93	}
94	
95	/// The `ochid:` value naming `chid` in `repo`, the URL read from its
96	/// `origin`.
97	pub fn ochid_value_for(
98	    repo: &std::path::Path,
99	    chid: &str,
100	) -> Result<String, Box<dyn std::error::Error>> {
101	    let url = crate::jj::remote_url(repo, "origin")?;
102	    Ok(ochid_value(url.as_deref(), &ochid_prefix_for(repo)?, chid))
103	}
104	
105	/// The `ochid:` value naming `chid` in `repo` by the side's label, the
106	/// form `--no-url-trailer` asks for.
107	pub fn ochid_label_value_for(
108	    repo: &std::path::Path,
109	    chid: &str,
110	) -> Result<String, Box<dyn std::error::Error>> {
111	    Ok(ochid_value(None, &ochid_prefix_for(repo)?, chid))
112	}
113	
114	/// The `ochid:` value naming `chid` in `repo`, by URL only when
115	/// `url_form`, so a partner follows the form its work commit took.
116	pub fn ochid_value_in_form(
117	    url_form: bool,
118	    repo: &std::path::Path,
119	    chid: &str,
120	) -> Result<String, Box<dyn std::error::Error>> {
121	    match url_form {
122	        true => ochid_value_for(repo, chid),
123	        false => ochid_label_value_for(repo, chid),
124	    }
125	}
126	
127	/// The placeholder `ocid:` value for a commit in `repo`, `None` when
128	/// it has no canonical URL, since the value is a link.
129	pub fn ocid_placeholder_for(
130	    repo: &std::path::Path,
131	) -> Result<Option<String>, Box<dyn std::error::Error>> {
132	    let url = crate::jj::remote_url(repo, "origin")?;
133	    Ok(url
134	        .as_deref()
135	        .and_then(crate::url::canonical_repo_url)
136	        .map(|url| format!("{url}/commit/{OCID_PLACEHOLDER}")))
137	}

139	/// A placeholder `ocid:` value with `sha` in its place, `None` when
140	/// `value` is not a placeholder, so one already set stays as it is.
141	pub fn ocid_with_sha(value: &str, sha: &str) -> Option<String> {
142	    value
143	        .strip_suffix(OCID_PLACEHOLDER)
144	        .and_then(|url| url.strip_suffix("/commit/"))
145	        .map(|url| format!("{url}/commit/{sha}"))
146	}

149	/// the line's place kept.

151	    desc.lines()

153	            true => format!("ocid: {value}"),

155	        })

158	}

164	}

# The package name is the installed binary's name and never
# changes: a cycle's validation installs under its own root,
# `--root tmp/dev` in `.vc-config.md`'s `[validate]` lists, so a
# dev build (a suffixed version) never replaces the stable
# `vc-x1` on the PATH. The promotion is the plain `cargo install`
# from `main`. Before 2026-10-20 a cycle renamed the package to
# `vc-x1-dev` instead, guarded by build.rs (chores-16, 0.78.3).

[lints.clippy]
# The process-spawn ban: `Command::new` is disallowed via
# clippy.toml's `disallowed-methods`, and deny (not warn) so a bare
# new spawn site fails `cargo clippy` even without `-D warnings`.
# The documented allowlist lives in clippy.toml.
disallowed_methods = "deny"

[dependencies]
chrono = { version = "0.4", default-features = false, features = ["now"] }
clap = { version = "4.6", features = ["derive", "wrap_help"] }
clap_complete = { version = "4.6", features = ["unstable-dynamic"] }
futures = "0.3"
# The gix jj-lib 0.46 resolves (no features of our own): the
# session's lock-contention downcast needs type identity with the
# errors jj-lib returns, and init's bare-repo creation reuses it.
gix = { version = "0.88", default-features = false }
# When raising jj-lib: check whether it now offers the commits a

jj-lib = "0.46"
log = { version = "0.4", features = ["std"] }
pollster = "1.0"
# The rng jj-lib's `SecureConfig` takes to mint a repo's config id,
# at jj-lib 0.46's versions so the types are its own, seeded the way
# jj-cli seeds it (src/jj/session.rs `load_repo_config`).
rand = "0.10"
rand_chacha = "0.10"
serde_json = "1"

[target.'cfg(unix)'.dependencies]

  first, by change id, each tree checked unchanged. The range defaults to the cycle's, and a commit on
  the trunk's remote needs `--yes`. A `lost` or short id is left as it is, with no `ocid:`.

  stays fluid, and the rest of this block's "keeps its placeholder" no longer holds.

Rung [8] is ready for your review. Full validation passed before the final record edits and fast validation after them, and the new code is installed as `vc-x1-dev`.

**What changed**
- **`ochid`:** it's now a bare change id on both sides. Readers also accept it, and every older form stays valid.
- **URL links:** with a hosted `origin`, a work commit carries `ocid` for the agent commit and `pcid` for each parent. `--no-url-trailer` leaves both out, so `ochid` is the only trailer stamped.
- **Agent first:** `-s b` and `init` now commit the agent side first, so `ocid` has the real SHA. A later `push` no longer folds the journal into that commit when `-s b` stamped an `ocid`, which is any hosted repo.
- **Custom trailers:** rewrites keep trailers they didn't stamp, so `custom.md` can add its own. A one-line body paragraph like `Solution: ...` stays body.
- **`vc-x1 trailers --update [--range <BM|REV>]`:** it updates a range oldest first and checks each tree is unchanged. A `lost` or short id is left alone, and commits on the trunk's remote need `--yes`.
- **Land:** it runs the same pass, but only refreshes links a commit already has. Published commits are now updated with a warning, replacing the `set_ocids` behaviour I flagged.

**Tried on this cycle** (dry runs, nothing changed)
`trailers --update --dry-run` would change all 8 commits, each to this shape:
```
ochid: qrxovvvqxnrq
ocid: https://github.com/winksaville/vc-x1.agent-session/commit/xxxx
pcid: https://github.com/winksaville/vc-x1/commit/<parent-sha>
```
The land dry run names all 8 work commits in the agent commit, and `validate-desc` still passes on the current ones.

**State of the repo**
- The closing is off the bookmark, so `origin` still has the old closing, `cd16d37d`, until a force-push that needs your go.
- `main` and the agent repo are untouched.
- The history tool is filed at the bottom of `## Todo`, and the Continuation notes have the new plan.

**Not done yet**
- `validate-desc` doesn't check that `ocid` and `pcid` name the right repo. I said the repo check would move to `ocid`, but it hasn't, and URL-form `ochid` keeps its check for now.
- `fix-desc` still writes the label form when it infers a missing trailer.
- `trailers --update` only changes the work repo, so a full history rewrite would need the agent side added.
- `-s w --push` still leaves `xxxx`, since only a land sets the SHA.
- A real `trailers --update` has only run in tests; this cycle's commits get it after the re-close.

**Decision for you**
The cycle's title, "feat: ochid trailers are URLs", now says the opposite of the result. I'd retitle it at the re-close, and that's left open in the notes. The ladder can carry on either way.

message.content: what's wrong with remote-work.git for wt3 and that's how the tests work?

content.text:
Nothing's wrong with it. `remote-work.git` is a perfectly good remote: you can push to it, sync with it, and land on it. It just can't produce a link, because `canonical_repo_url` deliberately returns nothing for a local path or `file://`. `ochid` works the same there, and `ocid` and `pcid` are left out.

The reason was the earlier design decision: a path like `/home/wink/...` only means something on one machine, and no browser could open it as `.../commit/<sha>`.

**And yes, that's how the tests work.** `Fixture` builds the same kind of local bare remotes, so most tests see no links at all. The ones that test links first point `origin` at a fake GitHub URL with `git remote set-url`, and never push to it. That has a weakness: the link code only runs in the tests written for it, not in the ordinary `commit`, `land` and `push` tests.

**To see links in `tmp/wt3` today,** do the same thing temporarily, then restore the original `origin`:
```bash
git -C tmp/wt3 remote set-url origin https://github.com/winksaville/wt3
git -C tmp/wt3/<agent-dir> remote set-url origin https://github.com/winksaville/wt3.agent-session
```
Commits and `trailers --update` will then stamp links, but pushes will fail until it's restored.

**The alternative** is to stamp links for local remotes too, using the path as the URL:
```
ocid: /home/wink/.../remote-work.agent-session.git/commit/<sha>
```
- **For:** `tmp/wt3` and every test fixture would run the same code as a hosted repo, which removes the weakness above, and tools could still read the repo and SHA from it.
- **Against:** the machine's paths end up in commit messages, and they'd stay there if that repo were later pushed to GitHub. That's what the design was avoiding.

**My recommendation:** keep it as it is, since those paths would be permanent once published. For test coverage, I'd have `Fixture` offer a hosted-URL setup and use it in the main `commit` and `land` flow tests. If you'd rather have local links, it's a small change in [8], so tell me and I'll make it; otherwise this question doesn't change anything in the rung.

```

In a dry run, `pcid` shows the parent's current SHA, because nothing is rewritten yet. The real run goes oldest first and uses each parent's new SHA. `vc-x1 validate` passes, and `vc-x1-dev` is installed from this code.

**Tests:** every fixture now runs the link code by default, which you wanted, and ten tests changed. Most just expected `ochid` to be the last line, but it also exposed two behaviours I hadn't tested:

1. **`squash` and `push` no longer fold the journal into a linked pair's agent commit.** A fold would change the SHA that `ocid` names. Both now have tests for this, and the old folding is tested on `--no-url-trailer` pairs.
2. **`squash --title --body` on a linked pair re-describes only the work commit,** for the same reason. The two commits' titles can then differ. It's recorded under "Not yet" in the rung, and `desc --title` won't change it, because any re-describe of an agent commit changes its SHA.

**The cost of `file:///`:** the machine's path is now in those commits' messages, and it stays there if a repo with a local `origin` is later pushed to GitHub. `trailers --update --range ...` can rewrite the links after `origin` changes, but only before the commits are widely shared. This doesn't affect this repo, whose `origin` is GitHub.

content.text:
`pcid` is my name for your idea, so you wouldn't recall the name. You never approved it specifically.

You suggested the work-repo URL "could have the parents", and I replied proposing `pcid`, short for Parent Commit ID, with one line per parent. You then said to continue, and I took that as agreement and built it. I should have called out the name as still needing your yes.

It's the link to a work commit's parent in the work repo:
```
ochid: qrxovvvqxnrq                                        # the agent change
ocid: https://github.com/winksaville/vc-x1.agent-session/commit/<sha>   # the agent commit
pcid: https://github.com/winksaville/vc-x1/commit/<parent-sha>          # this commit's parent
```

- **Why a parent:** it replaces the `wurl` I first proposed. A commit can't contain its own SHA, but it can contain its parent's, which names both the work repo and a real commit.
- **What it adds:** git already records parents, so within the repo it's redundant. It pays off when a commit is forked or cherry-picked, because the trailer still shows where it came from. It also gives you a clickable link to the parent.
- **How many:** one per parent, so a trapezoid's merge commit gets two, and a root commit gets none.
- **What it costs:** a rewrite changes a parent's SHA, so a land or `trailers --update` has to refresh every `pcid`, oldest first.

The name and the feature are both still yours to decide. It's only a few lines to rename it, or to drop it if a plain work-repo URL is what you meant. I'd keep the feature, since it records real provenance. The name is less clear-cut, because `pcid` only reads well next to `ocid`, so you may prefer something plainer like `parent:`.

  one agent commit naming them all.

A label names a side, not a repo, so nothing in a published commit says where its partner lives, and
anyone holding only the work-repo cannot resolve it. The URL carries that, and a change id rather
than a SHA survives a rewrite, which `ocid:` then adds for a reader in a browser.

### squash

Continue a rung: fold the working copies into the pair `commit` made. A review's fix in the work
`@` folds into the work commit, and the journal into the agent commit, each keeping its change id,
so both trailers stay right without being touched.

```
vc-x1 squash -s b                                    # both sides
vc-x1 squash -s w                                    # the work side only, a draft too
vc-x1 squash -s w --yes                              # a commit already on main's remote
vc-x1 squash -s b --title "feat: ..." --body @tmp/body.md   # and rewrite the descriptions
vc-x1 squash -s p -R ../other                        # a plain repo's @ into its @-
```

`-s` is required and `-R` optional. The agent side goes by where the partner stands: committed by
`commit -s b`, so the journal folds into it, or pending after `commit -s w`, so the journal already
is the partner and push commits it. A published side goes by where it was published:

- a draft, published on a topic bookmark only, is rewritten with a warning, since the cycle is not
  landed and the next push only moves its bookmark
- a commit on `main`'s remote is history others have, refused without `--yes`
- a published partner with only the journal to fold is left for push, whose agent half folds it

A work `@-` with no trailer is not a pair's. `--title` with `--body` rewrites the descriptions and
keeps each trailer, the one sanctioned re-describe of a trailer-carrying commit, warned or refused
as a fold is. `--dry-run` prints what it would fold and re-describe, and changes nothing.

[8] is committed, and rung [9], the docs, is ready for your review. `vc-x1 validate` passes, and `vc-x1-dev` is installed with the new help.

**Your question:** yes on both, now with tests.
- **Closing commit:** a test confirms it lists two `pcid` lines in parent order. A closing's first parent is the trunk.
- **N parents:** a new test builds a commit with three parents and checks three `pcid` lines in parent order.

**[9] changes**
- **README:**
  - The linking section now leads with bare `ochid`, then `ocid` and `pcid`, each with what it's for. Earlier forms are listed as still valid.
  - It also warns that a `file:///` path stays in the commit message.
  - `trailers` has its own section and an entry in the command list.
  - `commit`, `land`, `squash` and `init` say what they stamp, and that a linked agent commit doesn't get folded into.
- **`-h` and `--help`:**
  - `trailers` has full long help.
  - `land` no longer says a land always pushes.
  - `--no-url-trailer` describes the new meaning.
- **v0.3.1 proposal:**
  - **ochid trailers are URLs** is now **Work commits link by URL**, with a new "why".
  - **A cycle stays local until its Land** now says the land writes `pcid` too.

**Not changed:** `agent-data/jj.md` and `AGENTS.md` still describe the old form until the proposal runs, the same call I made in [7].

**Next, once you've approved [9]:**

2. Run `trailers --update` on the real commits, then `validate-desc` and `land --dry-run`.

content.text:
**Partly on the first, and no on the second.**

**Trailer styles (`ochid` only)**
- It accepts all the forms: bare, `/.claude/<id>`, `/<id>`, `/.agent-session/<id>` and `<repo-url>#<id>`. Run with the current build, it passes this cycle's 9 commits, 8 URL-form and 1 bare.
- **Gap:** it only checks the last `ochid` on a commit. A land's agent commit carries one per work commit, so on this cycle's agent commit it would check 1 of 9.
- There's also no unit test for the bare form; that real run is the only evidence.

**`ocid` and `pcid`**
It doesn't read them at all. I mentioned this as "not done yet" on [8], but it matters more now: a wrong or stale link passes `validate-desc` with `ok`.

**What I'd add**
These checks all work offline, from the local repos and their remote-tracking state:

| Trailer | Check | Result if wrong |
|---|---|---|
| every `ochid` | each one resolves, not just the last | issue |
| `ocid` | URL names the agent repo's `origin` | issue |
| `ocid` | SHA exists in the agent repo and is the commit `ochid` names | issue |
| `ocid` | `xxxx` is only allowed while `ochid` names the uncommitted agent `@` | issue |
| `pcid` | URL names the work repo's `origin` | issue |
| `pcid` | same count, same SHAs, same order as the commit's actual parents | issue |
| `ocid` | the agent commit isn't on `origin` yet | note, since that's normal before a push |

- **Old commits:** having no `ocid` or `pcid` isn't an error, so old commits and `--no-url-trailer` commits still pass.
- **The fix:** `trailers --update` repairs anything stale, and the message can say so.

**What "functional" can't mean by default:** actually fetching the URL. It needs a network, and a private repo returns 404 even when the link is right. An optional `--online` flag could do it later, but I'd leave that out for now. The checks above catch a link that points at the wrong place. Whether it opens in a browser only depends on the push.

**Where it goes:** I'd approve [9] as it stands and add a new rung, then close:

| Label | Rung |
|---|---|
| [9] | docs, as they are now |
| [10] | new: `validate-desc` checks every `ochid`, `ocid` and `pcid`, with its own docs |
| [11] | the closing |

That also gives the final `trailers --update` a real check before the force-push, which is what you want before landing.

Say go and I'll commit [9] and start [10].

Rung [10] is ready for your review. `vc-x1 validate` passes, and `vc-x1-dev` is installed from this code; the only edit after that run is a note in the record. [9] is committed at `4258069278b2`.

**What `validate-desc` now checks**
- **Every `ochid`** on a commit, not just the last one.
- **`ocid`:** the URL names the agent repo's `origin`. The SHA must be the commit `ochid` names, or `xxxx` only while that's still the uncommitted agent `@`.
- **`pcid`:** the URL names the work repo's `origin`, and the SHAs must match the commit's parents exactly: same count, same order.
- **Notes and exemptions:** an agent commit not yet on a remote shows as a `note`, not an error. A commit with no links passes, so old history is unaffected.
- **No fetching:** it's all offline, so a private repo's link can't be told apart from a broken one. The README says so.

**Two bugs it found, both fixed**
1. **`-s w --push` left `xxxx`:** the push commits the agent side, so the placeholder was stale and failed the new check. `push` now sets the real SHA when it has just made that commit and `@-` is unpublished. That also removes one of the "not yet" items from [8].
2. **A sentence read as a trailer:** old commit `ltwrzrmvoxtn` has a body line starting `ochid: trailers. A squash...` at column 0. Checking every `ochid` flagged it, and a rewrite would have deleted that sentence. A stamped trailer's value must now be one word, so it stays body text.

**Checked on real repos**

| Repo and range | Result |
|---|---|
| This cycle, last 10 work commits | all `ok` |
| `main`, work repo | identical to the landed 0.85.17 |
| `main`, agent repo | same counts as 0.85.17 (19 issues, all there before), with more detail on those lines |
| `tmp/wt3` | all `ok` (checked before the two fixes above) |

The agent repo's old commits with several bad `ochid`s now list each kind of problem once.

**Test coverage**
Unit tests cover each wrong-link case, `pcid` order on a merge, the `note`, and a wrong link failing the whole run. The checks haven't yet seen a real `pcid` set on a whole cycle, or a real SHA in an `ocid`; that comes with the final `trailers --update`.

**Next, once you've approved [10]:** re-close as `feat: improve trailers`, run `trailers --update`, then `validate-desc` and `land --dry-run`, and stop for your go on the force-push.

content.text:
Not quite. `commit --closing ... --land` comes closest, but no single command does all of it. Your output looks right, by the way: the two `miss` lines are just the uncommitted `@` in each repo.

From reading the code (I haven't run these on a real cycle):

| Command | Agent commit | Links | Old trailer forms |
|---|---|---|---|
| `commit -s w --closing BM` | not made | closing gets `xxxx` | not touched |
| `commit -s b --closing BM` | names **only the closing** | closing gets the real SHA, rungs keep `xxxx` | not touched |
| `commit -s w\|b --closing BM --land` | names **every** work commit | all set, oldest first | not touched |
| `land -s b --onto T` | names every work commit | all set, oldest first | not touched |
| `trailers --update` | not made | all refreshed | moved to today's form |

**Two gaps**
1. **`-s b --closing` without `--land` is a trap:** it commits the agent side naming only the closing, so the rungs keep `xxxx` while their agent commit already exists. `validate-desc` would now flag every one of them, and `trailers --update` would be the repair.
2. **`--land` doesn't move old trailer forms:** its pass only refreshes the links a commit already has, so a commit with no links stays that way. That's fine for a cycle stamped by this build, and this cycle only needed `trailers --update` because its early rungs predate the protocol.

**What I'd build**
Make `--closing -s b` the complete closing of both repos, with no separate trailer step:
1. Commit the agent side first, with one `ochid` per work commit naming it, the closing included. Its chid is already known.
2. Make the closing with the real `ocid` SHA and both `pcid`s.
3. Run the trailer pass over the whole range, moving old forms and setting every link, unless `--no-url-trailer` was given.

Then the flags add one step each:
